fuller.text: This encyclopedia article covers the dodo, an extinct bird that could not fly and lived only on Mauritius, an island in the Indian Ocean. It belonged to the pigeon and dove family, and its closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon. The article gathers what is known about its looks, life, extinction, remains and fame.

fuller.text: The article says the dodo matters because it died out less than a century after people first recorded it in 1598. That loss drew attention to a problem nobody had noticed before: humans can wipe out whole species. Since 1833 it has served as an example of human-caused extinction, and it is called an "icon of extinction".

fuller.text: The evidence is thin, which shapes everything else in the article. No complete preserved bird exists, so its living appearance comes mainly from 17th-century drawings, paintings and written accounts. A dried head at Oxford is the only soft tissue left, beside a few bones from birds brought to Europe. Most bones come from the Mare aux Songes swamp, which yielded remains of over 300 dodos.

fuller.text: Early scientists guessed it was an ostrich, a vulture or other birds. Studies of a skull and of the Oxford head and foot in the 1840s showed it was a kind of pigeon. DNA work in 2002 linked it to the Nicobar pigeon and to the Rodrigues solitaire, another extinct flightless bird. But that DNA came from one damaged specimen, so the article says these results still need checking.

fuller.text: Dodos stood about 62.6 to 75 cm tall, and males were larger than females. Weight estimates differ, with one study giving 10.6 to 17.5 kg for wild birds. The famous fat, clumsy image may come from overfed captive birds or badly stuffed ones. A 2016 brain study found its brain-to-body size matched modern pigeons, so it was probably about as smart.

fuller.text: Little is known of how it lived, but the article pieces together several likely habits. It probably ate fallen fruit, nuts, seeds, bulbs and roots. Several old accounts say it swallowed stones to help grind up food in its gut. A 2017 study of thin bone slices suggests it bred around August, and chicks grew fast.

fuller.text: Contrary to popular belief, hunting by sailors was probably not the main cause of its extinction. Animals people brought, especially pigs and macaques, raided nests and competed for food, while forests were cut down. The last widely accepted sighting is from 1662, though a 2003 statistical study estimated 1693. Some later reports may describe the red rail, another flightless bird that took over the dodo's name.

fuller.text: The article concludes the exact date may never be settled, but the dodo was probably gone by 1700. Its main lesson is that a bird long mocked as fat and clumsy is now thought to have been well suited to its home.

brief.text: This encyclopedia article is about the dodo, a flightless bird that lived only on Mauritius. Mauritius is an island in the Indian Ocean, and the dodo was a large relative of pigeons. It is often shown as fat and clumsy, but it was probably well suited to its home.

brief.text: Dutch sailors first wrote about the dodo in 1598. The last widely accepted sighting was in 1662. Hunting was not the main cause; animals brought by people and forest loss are thought to have mattered more. Its quick disappearance made people notice that humans can wipe out whole species.
